lead: Every neuron adds up its inputs into a weighted sum z, then passes z through an activation function f. That function adds the bend that makes depth useful, and its derivative decides how much gradient flows back during training. This chapter gives the formula, range and derivative of sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and leaky ReLU, then softmax for the output layer, and says which one belongs where. Getting this choice right is half of making a network train at all.
prereq: You need the multilayer perceptron and the argument for non-linear activations from 1.6.

sections.h3: Why a bend is needed, and sigmoid

blocks.text: A unit adds up its inputs, z = Σᵢ wᵢxᵢ + b, where xᵢ are the inputs, wᵢ their weights and b the bias. Passing z straight on gains nothing: a weighted sum of weighted sums is still one weighted sum. The activation function f inserts a bend, a = f(z), and that bend is what makes a stack of layers stronger than one layer (see 1.6).
f must be non-linear, and it must have a usable derivative, because backpropagation sends error backwards multiplied by f′(z): the derivative decides how much gradient each unit passes on (see 1.9).

blocks.where: z is the weighted sum w·x + b; e ≈ 2.718 is Euler's number; σ(z) is the unit's output.

blocks.text: Sigmoid, also called the logistic function, squeezes any real number into (0, 1). Its derivative is σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), at most 0.25, reached at z = 0. At z = 10 the output is 0.99995 and the derivative about 0.00005: the curve saturates at both ends, so a deep stack of sigmoid units passes almost no gradient. Outputs are never negative, so the unit is not zero-centred, and the weight updates of a unit tend to push the same way, which slows learning.
Sigmoid survives in the output layer of a yes/no classifier, where a number in (0, 1) reads as a probability (see 1.8).

blocks.where: z is the weighted sum; the output lies in (−1, 1); the derivative is 1 − tanh²(z), at most 1 at z = 0.

blocks.text: tanh is sigmoid stretched and shifted. It is zero-centred, which suits hidden layers better than sigmoid, but it still saturates at both ends, so very deep tanh stacks learn slowly too.

blocks.where: z is the weighted sum; the output lies in [0, ∞); the derivative is 1 for z > 0 and 0 for z < 0, and is taken as 0 at z = 0 by convention.

blocks.text: ReLU is zero for negative z and the identity for positive z. It costs one comparison, and on the positive side it never saturates, so a gradient of exactly 1 flows back through an active unit. That is why deep networks train at all. The catch is the dying unit: a ReLU whose z is negative for every training example outputs 0 and receives gradient 0, so its weights never move again.
f(z) = z if z > 0, and αz if z ≤ 0
blocks.where: α is a small positive slope, α > 0, typically 0.01 or 0.1 (α = 0.1 is used in the figure and the example); the derivative is 1 for z > 0 and α for z < 0.

blocks.text: Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope below zero, so a unit still gets a gradient when z < 0 and a dead unit can recover. ReLU is the default for hidden layers of feed-forward and convolutional networks; leaky ReLU is a cheap safety net.

sections.h3: Softmax for the whole output vector

blocks.where: z = (z₁, …, z_K) are the K class scores from the last layer, zᵢ is the score of class i, and pᵢ is the predicted probability of class i.

blocks.text: Each pᵢ lies in (0, 1) and the pᵢ sum to 1, so the outputs read as the model's belief over K classes. Softmax belongs in the output layer of a single-label classifier, paired with cross-entropy loss (see 1.8).

Softmax is not elementwise: every pᵢ depends on all the scores, so it cannot be applied unit by unit, and it has no place in a hidden layer. Subtracting the largest score from every zᵢ leaves the pᵢ unchanged but avoids overflow in e^zᵢ. The ranking survives: the largest score gets the largest probability.

figure.caption: Each curve is drawn from z = −4 to 4 with its values at z = 2 and z = −2 marked. Sigmoid and tanh flatten at both ends, ReLU is 0 for negative z, and leaky ReLU keeps a slope of 0.1 there.

spec.aria: Four small plots of sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and leaky ReLU from z equals −4 to 4, each with its values at z = 2 and z = −2 marked.

examples.question: A hidden unit sees a weighted sum z = 2 in one example and z = −2 in another. Evaluate sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and leaky ReLU (α = 0.1) at both, and give the derivative of each at z = 2. A 3-class output layer then produces scores z = (2, 1, 0); find the softmax probabilities and check that they sum to 1.
steps: ReLU at z = 2 gives max(0, 2) = 2; at z = −2 gives max(0, −2) = 0.
Leaky ReLU at z = 2 gives 2; at z = −2 gives 0.1 × (−2) = −0.2.
Softmax: e² = 7.389, e¹ = 2.718, e⁰ = 1.000; the sum is 11.107.
examples.answer: The activations at z = 2 and z = −2 are sigmoid 0.881 and 0.119, tanh 0.964 and −0.964, ReLU 2 and 0, leaky ReLU 2 and −0.2; softmax of (2, 1, 0) is (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), which sums to 1.000.
examples.check:
import math
sig = lambda z: 1/(1+math.exp(-z))
relu = lambda z: max(0.0, z)
leaky = lambda z: z if z > 0 else 0.1*z
vals = [sig(2), sig(-2), math.tanh(2), math.tanh(-2), relu(2), relu(-2), leaky(2), leaky(-2)]
z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0]
s = sum(math.exp(v) for v in z)
p = [math.exp(v)/s for v in z]
for v in vals + p:
    print(round(v, 3))

traps: Applying softmax element by element. It needs the whole vector, because every output depends on all the scores.
Forgetting that σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) is at most 0.25. Deep sigmoid stacks learn slowly for exactly this reason; examiners like asking for the maximum and where it occurs (z = 0).
Calling sigmoid zero-centred. Its outputs are in (0, 1); tanh is the zero-centred one, in (−1, 1).
Writing ReLU′(0) as a fact. It is undefined at 0; convention sets it to 0 or 1, and either is acceptable if stated.
Mixing up leaky ReLU and dying ReLU: the leak exists to stop units dying, and with α = 0.1 at z = −2 it gives −0.2, not 0.

quiz.q: State the range and the derivative of the sigmoid function.
quiz.a: Range (0, 1); derivative σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), maximum 0.25 at z = 0.

quiz.q: Why does a stack of many sigmoid layers learn slowly compared with ReLU layers?
quiz.a: Sigmoid saturates, and its derivative is at most 0.25. Backpropagation multiplies many such small factors, so the gradient reaching the early layers shrinks sharply. ReLU has derivative exactly 1 for z > 0, so the product does not shrink on the active side.

quiz.q: A leaky ReLU has α = 0.1. Give its output and derivative at z = −3.
Find the softmax probabilities of the scores z = (0, 0, 0).
quiz.a: Each e⁰ = 1, sum = 3, so p = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) ≈ (0.333, 0.333, 0.333). Equal scores give equal probabilities.

quiz.q: A hidden ReLU unit has negative z for every training example. Explain what happens to its gradient and weights, and how leaky ReLU changes the outcome.
quiz.a: Its output is 0 and its derivative is 0, so the gradient through it is 0 for every example and its weights never change: the unit is dead. Leaky ReLU gives derivative α (a small positive number, α = 0.1 here) on the negative side, so a small non-zero gradient still reaches the weights and the unit can recover.

quiz.q: Why is softmax unsuitable for a hidden layer?
quiz.a: Softmax couples all units, so one unit's output depends on every other unit's score; it also forces the outputs to sum to 1, creating competition between hidden units that is not wanted. Hidden layers need a per-unit non-linearity, applied to each z separately.

quiz.q: Why is softmax computed after subtracting the maximum score?
quiz.a: Adding the same constant to every zᵢ cancels in the ratio e^zᵢ/Σⱼ e^zⱼ, so the probabilities are unchanged. Subtracting the maximum keeps the largest exponent at 0, which prevents overflow when the scores are large.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern practice adds more shapes: GELU and SiLU (also called swish) are smooth curves that behave like ReLU for large positive z but keep a small gradient below zero, and transformers commonly use GELU. Some models learn the activation itself, as in PReLU, where α is trained. Softmax has a temperature parameter in language models, dividing every score by T before exponentiating, which controls how peaked the distribution is. Search next for GELU, SiLU and temperature scaling.
